clinicalPearls: The most common form is a distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy that begins in the feet and progresses proximally in a stocking-and-glove distribution
Sensory loss predisposes to unnoticed foot injury, ulceration, and Charcot arthropathy, making regular foot examination essential
Painful neuropathy can coexist with sensory loss, causing burning, tingling, and allodynia that are often worse at night
Autonomic involvement can produce postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so other causes of neuropathy such as vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol, uraemia, and hypothyroidism should be considered
Optimised glycaemic control is central to prevention and slowing progression, particularly in type 1 diabetes
Management of painful neuropathy relies on agents active in neuropathic pain rather than simple analgesics, alongside foot protection strategies
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages peripheral nerves through several linked mechanisms, including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, activation of the polyol and protein kinase C pathways, oxidative stress, and microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum. These processes injure axons and Schwann cells, producing a length-dependent loss of both small and large fibres. Involvement of autonomic fibres disrupts cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary regulation, while focal ischaemia or entrapment can cause mononeuropathies and radiculopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 or other nutritional deficiency neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Clinical foot examination with monofilament and vibration testing
HbA1c and glucose assessment to gauge control
Serum vitamin B12, thyroid function, and renal function to exclude alternative causes
Nerve conduction studies in atypical or asymmetric presentations
Autonomic function testing including orthostatic blood pressure measurement when indicated
redFlags: Foot ulceration, deformity, or signs of Charcot arthropathy
Rapidly progressive, asymmetric, or predominantly motor deficits suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Severe autonomic features such as symptomatic postural hypotension or gastroparesis
Signs of limb ischaemia or infection complicating a neuropathic foot
reference.prognosis: Neuropathy tends to progress with duration and poor control of diabetes, and established nerve damage is largely irreversible, so the emphasis is on prevention of ulceration and amputation and on symptom control; autonomic neuropathy carries an adverse cardiovascular prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing all neuropathy to diabetes without excluding treatable alternative causes
Neglecting routine foot inspection and patient education, allowing preventable ulcers
Undertreating painful neuropathy or relying on ineffective simple analgesics
Missing autonomic neuropathy as the cause of unexplained postural symptoms or gastrointestinal complaints
